power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

text.text: Regional volumetric assessment of perinatal brain development is currently limited by the lack of consistent high quality multi-regional segmentation methods applicable to both fetal and neonatal MRI.
We present Multi-BOUNTI, a deep learning pipeline for automated multi-lobe segmentation of fetal and neonatal T2w brain MRI.
The method is based on a dedicated 43-label parcellation protocol and a 3D Attention UNet trained on brain MRI datasets of subjects spanning 21-44 weeks gestational/postmenstrual age.

The pipeline integrates preprocessing, segmentation and volumetric analysis, and was evaluated on independent datasets, demonstrating fast (< 10 min/case) and accurate performance with high agreement to manually refined labels.
text.formatted: The pipeline integrates preprocessing, segmentation and volumetric analysis, and was evaluated on independent datasets, demonstrating fast (< 10 min/case) and accurate performance with high agreement to manually refined labels.

text.text: We demonstrate the application of the framework with 267 fetal and 593 neonatal MRI datasets from the developing Human Connectome Project without reported clinically significant brain anomalies to derive normative volumetric growth models across 21-44 weeks GA/PMA.
These models were used to characterise developmental trajectories, assess differences between fetal and preterm neonatal cohorts, and analyse longitudinal changes.
The resulting normative models were integrated into an automated reporting framework enabling subject-specific volumetric assessment via centiles and z-scores.
Multi-BOUNTI provides a unified and scalable approach for perinatal brain segmentation and volumetry, supporting large-scale studies and facilitating future clinical translation.
The full pipeline is publicly available at https://github.com/SVRTK/perinatal-brain-mri-analysis.

text.text: Automated segmentation of brain structures is a key component of modern fetal and neonatal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) studies of brain development, supporting both exploratory research and clinical applications.

Typically performed on structural T2-weighted (T2w) MRI, it provides regional volumetric measurements for normative modelling (Dimitrova et al., 2021; Cromb et al., 2024) and serves as an essential input for cortical surface analysis (Ma et al., 2025), quantitative MRI relaxometry (Payette et al., 2025b), as well as a key component of functional and diffusion MRI processing pipelines for connectomic analysis.
text.formatted: Typically performed on structural T2-weighted (T2w) MRI, it provides regional volumetric measurements for normative modelling <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Dimitrova et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Cromb et al., 2024)</ref> and serves as an essential input for cortical surface analysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Ma et al., 2025)</ref>, quantitative MRI relaxometry <ref type="bibr">(Payette et al., 2025b)</ref>, as well as a key component of functional and diffusion MRI processing pipelines for connectomic analysis.

text.text: Automated volumetric assessment of abnormal anatomy (Deprest et al., 2023) also has strong potential for integration into clinical radiological workflows, which still predominantly rely on manual 2D biometry of major brain structures.

text.text: Consequently, both segmentation quality and the anatomical fidelity of parcellation protocols directly affect downstream analysis.
Introduced over a decade ago, classical registrationbased pipelines for 3D fetal and neonatal brain segmentation remain the predominant reference standard.

The Draw-EM pipeline (Makropoulos et al., 2018), developed within the developing Human Connectome Project (dHCP) (Edwards et al., 2022), uses ALBERT atlas label propagation and expectation maximisation clustering, enabling the first standardised multi-regional (87 labels) segmentation of large fetal and neonatal cohorts and has been widely adopted.

text.text: Similarly, the CRL fetal brain atlases with more than 100 regions (Gholipour et al., 2017; Bagheri et al., 2026) are widely used for label propagation and downstream analysis in many studies.

text.text: However, these classical approaches are typically associated with prolonged runtime, overestimation of the cortical ribbon and reduced registration accuracy in low-quality images and atypical anatomy, such as preterm neonates or severe anomalies.

More recently, Draw-EM and CRL atlas label propagation segmentations have been used to train 3D deep learning (DL) models, such as 3D UNet (Cicek et al., 2016) or nnUNet (Isensee et al., 2021), for T2w fetal (Huang et al., 2026; Zeng et al., 2026; Bagheri et al., 2026) and neonatal (Grigorescu et al., 2021; Richter and Fetit, 2022; Henschel et al., 2024; Mihailov et al., 2025) MRI.

text.text: Although these approaches offer substantially improved computational efficiency, errors and biases present in the training labels inherently propagate to the DL outputs.

The FeTA fetal brain segmentation challenge (Payette et al., 2025a) has led to multiple methods, including approaches targeting abnormal brain segmentation with varying image quality and acquisition protocols (Deprest et al., 2023; Fidon et al., 2024; Zalevskyi et al., 2026); however, the associated parcellation protocol is limited to eight global regions of interest (ROIs), and the manual ground truth labels contain inaccuracies.

text.text: We have recently described the BOUNTI fetal brain DL segmentation pipeline (Uus et al., 2023) partially addresses these limitations by using high-quality manually refined labels for training, but remains restricted to 19 parcellation ROIs, lacks lobewise subdivision of grey and white matter, and is not applicable to neonatal MRI.

text.text: To the best of our knowledge, no existing DL-based methods provide high-quality multi-lobe detailed segmentation applicable to both fetal and neonatal brain MRI.
This limitation is particularly relevant given the need for harmonised analysis across the perinatal period to enable continuous modelling of developmental trajectories (Urru et al., 2025).
text.formatted: This limitation is particularly relevant given the need for harmonised analysis across the perinatal period to enable continuous modelling of developmental trajectories <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Urru et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, including more regions may lead to increased understanding of brain development.

Here we address the need for a harmonised multi-lobe segmentation tool by introducing a prototype deep learning framework for combined fetal and neonatal multi-lobe brain segmentation of structural 3D T2w MRI.

The approach is based on a dedicated 43-label parcellation protocol specifically designed to ensure clinical and research relevance across the perinatal period, from the late second trimester to postnatal stages.

The pipeline integrates preprocessing with a 3D Attention UNet trained on 160 fetal and neonatal scans and evaluated on 40 datasets, with qualitative comparison to existing multilobe segmentation methods.

Next, we demonstrate a key application of our approach by deriving normative perinatal volumetric growth models across 21-44 weeks gestational (GA) and postmenstrual age (PMA) from 267 fetal and 593 neonatal (term and preterm) dHCP datasets without reported clinically significant brain findings.

These models are integrated into an automated reporting framework for subjectspecific volumetric assessment, providing percentiles and z-scores in .html format for potential clinical and research applications.

text.text: Region selection was guided by clinical and research relevance, as well as the visibility of ROI interfaces and anatomical landmarks on T2w contrast across the 21-44 weeks age range.

Due to rapid developmental changes and variable image quality, certain anatomical boundaries (e.g., major sulci before 24 weeks GA or the internal capsule separating deep grey matter structures) may not be well defined due to low visibility.
Where required for downstream analysis, these interfaces were approximated based on expected anatomical location.

The protocol was defined using atlas label propagation followed by manual sub-parcellation and refinement in 4 fetal and 4 neonatal datasets spanning 21-44 weeks GA using ITK-SNAP (Yushkevich et al., 2006).

text.text: The final protocol comprises 43 labels.
Cortical grey matter (GM) and white matter (WM) are subdivided into six major lobar ROIs per hemisphere (frontal, parietal, temporal, occipital, insular and cingulate).
Deep GM is partitioned into three regions per hemisphere (caudate nucleus, basal ganglia and thalami).

The intracranial cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) compartment includes perhemisphere extracerebral CSF and lateral ventricles, as well as the cavum (combined cavum septum pellucidum and vergae) and the third and fourth ventricles.
The posterior fossa is divided into brainstem, cerebellar hemispheres and vermis, and the corpus callosum is segmented as a single label.

As in Draw-EM, an additional intracerebral background label captures subcortical/diencephalic structures not explicitly delineated (e.g., internal capsule, hypothalamus, hippocampus), which are planned for further subdivision in future protocol extensions.

Predicted segmentations are transformed back to native space for downstream analysis.

text.text: In addition, we quantitatively assessed cortical grey matter segmentation, the one label defined consistently across all protocols.
For each subject, cortical GM was manually delineated on a single representative mid-axial slice in ITK-SNAP by one rater (AU).
Each method's output, including Multi-BOUNTI, was restricted to the same slice and binarised to cortical GM.

It was then compared with the manual reference using the Dice similarity coefficient, the 95th percentile Hausdorff distance, the average symmetric surface distance, and the relative volume differences.
All metrics were computed in 2D within the annotated slice.

text.text: All segmentations underwent visual quality control (AU, AFG).
Extracted regional volumetric and cortical metrics (left/right hemisphere structures were combined) were used to characterise developmental trajectories across the perinatal period.
Statistical analysis was performed in Python using statsmodels.

Analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) assessed associations with age at scan, sex, parental ethnicity, birth weight centile, and mode of delivery (neonates), as well as group differences between fetal and preterm neonatal cohorts.
Developmental effects were modelled using linear and quadratic terms of GA and PMA at scan.
Multiple comparisons across ROIs were controlled using Bonferroni correction.
Normative growth models were then derived to enable subject-specific estimation of centiles and z-scores.
Model fitting was performed separately for fetal and neonatal cohorts, with the latter including both term and preterm neonates to ensure continuity across the age range.
The 5th, 50th, and 95th centiles were estimated using polynomial regression (NumPy/SciPy), following established perinatal modelling approaches (Royston and Wright, 1998).

text.text: Finally, longitudinal analysis was performed in a subset of 10 subjects with three or four fetal and neonatal scan timepoints.
Growth rates were estimated using finite differences (∆volume/∆age) between consecutive scans, where age denotes GA for fetal and PMA for neonatal scans, and summarised across subjects.
Integration of the proposed segmentation pipeline into clinical workflows requires an intuitive and interpretable output format to support case-specific analysis.
Following segmentation, the 3D T2w image and corresponding segmentation are passed to a dedicated Python script (fetal or neonatal), which automatically generates an .html report.

The report includes: • general case information (patient identifier, scan date, GA/PMA); • 21 representative T2w images with segmentation overlays (axial, coronal and sagittal views); • tabulated measurements with observed-to-expected ratios, centiles and z-scores; • growth charts comparing extracted measurements to normative centile curves; • a disclaimer indicating research-only use pending regulatory approval for clinical deployment.
To explore the generalisability of Multi-BOUNTI beyond its training data, we performed two additional qualitative evaluations.

First, the pipeline was applied to an independent iFIND data release cohort comprising 405 reconstructed fetal brain MRI datasets acquired at 1.5T, including normal and abnormal cases, predominantly with cardiovascular anomalies, and varying image quality.

All segmentations were visually inspected (by AU) and assigned a quality grade based on the presence and severity of segmentation errors: (1) severe errors, (2) significant errors, (3) minor errors, or (4) good quality.

This assessment provided an initial evaluation of generalisation to different acquisition protocols and anatomical presentations, given that the pipeline was trained predominantly on normal anatomy from the dHCP 3T acquisition protocol.

Second, we presented representative segmentation examples for fetal and neonatal datasets with reported clinically significant anomaly findings to illustrate the method's performance in the presence of abnormal anatomy.

These examples included nine fetal and neonatal T2w reconstructions from the dHCP and iFIND cohorts (excluded from training) and three abnormal fetal brain MRI reconstructions from the FeTA challenge cohort (Payette et al., 2025a).

text.text: As expected, pronounced age-related changes in cortical folding are observed, together with gradual shifts in the relative proportions of the cerebellum and lateral ventricles.
Notably, cortical GM and WM exhibit similar visual appearance at overlapping fetal and neonatal time points (e.g., 30 and 38 weeks).

During protocol development, particular emphasis was placed on accurate delineation of cortical folds and exclusion of small CSF pockets and vascular regions, which are commonly misclassified due to similar intensity and partial volume effects in the existing methods.
The resulting parcellation provides a consistent global anatomical framework that can be further extended, including finer sub-parcellation of lobes and intracerebral background structures.
Evaluation on 20 fetal and 20 neonatal independent datasets (21-45 weeks age at scan), summarised in Fig. 3, demonstrates the feasibility and efficiency of the proposed pipeline.

text.text: Per-label qualitative scores were predominantly in the 3-4 range (acceptable-good), with 142 (8.26%) minor imperfections (grade 3) and 8 (0.47%) significant or severe errors (grades 1-2) across 1,720 case-specific label assessments (40 datasets x 43 labels).

These occurred mainly in cortical GM (frontal, parietal, temporal, occipital), cerebellar hemispheres, lateral ventricles and extracerebral CSF, primarily due to reduced contrast, limited regional visibility or vascular signal.
Despite these local inaccuracies, the predicted segmentations showed high agreement with manually refined labels, with small relative volumetric differences and high Dice scores across most regions.
Manual corrections required less than 2 minutes per case.

text.text: Across both populations, Multi-BOUNTI demonstrated more consistent anatomical delineation across ROIs, particularly around the ventricular system, deep grey matter and cortical boundaries.

Differences were especially apparent in cortical grey matter, where several existing methods showed overestimation of the cortical ribbon, inclusion of adjacent white matter or CSF, and less accurate delineation of cortical folding.
In contrast, Multi-BOUNTI provided a thinner and more anatomically consistent cortical ribbon, with improved correspondence to the underlying tissue boundaries.

These observations were consistent across the representative developmental stages, suggesting improved robustness to the substantial changes in brain morphology and cortical maturation across the fetal-neonatal period.

text.text: Multi-BOUNTI achieved the best performance across the evaluated cortical GM segmentation metrics in the three fetal and three neonatal test cases.

For neonatal MRI, it achieved a Dice coefficient of 0.865 ± 0.023, HD95 of 0.638 ± 0.120, ASSD of 0.259 ± 0.062 mm and relative volume difference of 2.616 ± 2.674%, outperforming all four comparison methods.

Similarly, for fetal MRI, Multi-BOUNTI achieved a Dice coefficient of 0.876 ± 0.018, HD95 of 0.569 ± 0.120, ASSD of 0.223 ± 0.058 mm and relative volume difference of 5.335 ± 3.423%, again providing the best results across all metrics.

The improvements in both volumetric overlap and surface-based measures indicate more accurate cortical boundary delineation, while the substantially lower volume differences suggest reduced over-and under-segmentation.
Together, these findings provide quantitative evidence supporting the improved cortical delineation observed visually in the evaluated fetal and neonatal datasets.

text.text: Cortical GM and WM volumes increased consistently across longitudinal timepoints, following subject-specific trajectories broadly aligned with the cross-sectional normative curves.
Centile values were largely preserved within similar ranges, with modest within-subject variation.

Growth rates were regionspecific, with highest in frontal GM (∼ 2.05 cc/week), followed by parietal (∼ 1.42), temporal (∼ 1.22), and occipital (∼ 1.02), while subcortical structures grew more slowly (e.g., thalamus ∼ 0.34), and cerebellar growth remained relatively high (∼ 1.02).
In contrast, CSF compartments showed more variable dynamics.
Extracerebral CSF volume generally increased with age, although growth rates were more variable, while lateral ventricles exhibited low growth rates (∼ 0.07 cc/week) and bidirectional changes.
Cavum volume remained largely stable or decreased (∼ 0.01 cc/week), consistent with involution.
Overall, parenchymal growth was consistent and generally accelerated with age with preserved scaling, whereas fluid compartments showed greater variability and less structured trajectories.

While the segmentations generally preserve the anatomical organisation of major brain regions, local inaccuracies are observed in areas affected by pronounced structural abnormalities or altered tissue appearance.
These examples illustrate the potential of Multi-BOUNTI for analysing abnormal fetal and neonatal brain MRI, while highlighting limitations in regions with atypical anatomy.
This work presents a deep learning framework that allows automated multi-lobe segmentation of T2w perinatal brain MRI across both fetal and neonatal periods.

It builds on the Draw-EM pipeline (Makropoulos et al., 2018) and the large dHCP cohort of T2w datasets (Edwards et al., 2022), providing fast, robust segmentation and integrated normative volumetry modelling.
text.formatted: It builds on the Draw-EM pipeline <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Makropoulos et al., 2018)</ref> and the large dHCP cohort of T2w datasets <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Edwards et al., 2022)</ref>, providing fast, robust segmentation and integrated normative volumetry modelling.

text.text: To ensure clinical and research relevance under realistic imaging constraints, we developed a dedicated parcellation protocol comprising 43 anatomical ROIs through consensus between neuroradiologists and imaging scientists.
Based on this protocol, the Multi-BOUNTI pipeline enables automated segmentation of fetal and neonatal T2w MRI and generation of volumetric reports.
The segmentation framework combines automated preprocessing (brain localisation and standard space alignment) with a 3D Attention UNet trained on 160 fetal and neonatal datasets.
Ground truth labels were generated using an iterative active learning strategy with manual refinement.

Evaluation on 40 independent datasets (20-45 weeks age at scan) demonstrated consistently high agreement with manually refined segmentations, with relative volumetric differences below 1% and high qualitative scores across the 43 labels.

The pipeline is publicly available (https://github.com/SVRTK/perinatal-brain-mri-analysis) and processes each case in under 10 minutes, supporting large-scale applications and suitability for clinical reporting timeframes.

Due to the imbalance in ethnic representation across cohorts, interpretation of the impact of parental ethnicity was in- herently limited.

Lobe-specific analysis of GM, WM, cortical surface area and gyrification index demonstrated preserved inter-regional relationships across development and the fetal-neonatal transition, consistent with findings from longitudinal analysis.

These data were used to derive normative volumetric growth models for fetal and neonatal brain development, enabling computation of subject-specific centiles and zscores within an automated reporting framework.
The resulting .html reports, incorporating segmentation overlays, tabulated measurements and growth charts, were reviewed by expert perinatal neuroradiologists and considered clinically relevant.
This supports the feasibility of integrating 3D segmentation-derived metrics into routine radiological reporting workflows in addition to standard 2D biometry.
Clinical significance of these improved phenotypes would need to be determined in further studies.
The reported centiles and z-scores provide age-specific reference measurements rather than diagnostic classification.
Furthermore, the normative models are specific to the Multi-BOUNTI parcellation protocol, and measurements derived using other segmentation methods may not be directly comparable.

Overall, the proposed Multi-BOUNTI pipeline provides a scalable baseline framework for unified fetal and neonatal brain segmentation and quantitative analysis, supporting both large-scale research studies and clinically interpretable volumetric assessment.

A key limitation is that training was performed exclusively on dHCP datasets acquired on a 3T scanner with specific acquisition parameters (e.g., TE=250 ms for fetal MRI), high image quality, and predominantly typically developing anatomy.

Nevertheless, qualitative evaluation on 405 independent 1.5T fetal MRI reconstructions from the iFIND cohort demonstrated generally good segmentation quality, suggesting promising generalisability across acquisition protocols without dedicated retraining of the segmentation model.
Further generalisation will require systematic validation across a wider range of acquisition protocols and image qualities.

This will necessitate expansion of the training cohort to include more heterogeneous datasets with possible application of harmonisation (Grigorescu et al., 2021) and synthetic learning (Billot et al., 2023; Valabregue et al., 2024) strategies.

text.text: Although a subset of abnormal cases from the dHCP cohort was included in training, this was not systematic and does not cover the full spectrum of fetal and neona-tal brain anomalies.

Nevertheless, representative examples of congenital malformations and acquired brain injuries showed that Multi-BOUNTI can delineate major anatomical structures across a range of abnormal presentations, suggesting potential applicability to pathological datasets.

However, these initial observations require further systematic validation and dedicated retraining using clinically representative pathological datasets to improve robustness across different types and severities of abnormalities.
Importantly, segmentation performance is inherently dependent on input image quality.
Severe motion artefacts, low signal-to-noise ratio, reconstruction errors and poorly defined anatomical boundaries may intrinsically limit segmentation accuracy, independently of model performance.
These image-quality-related limitations should be distinguished from model-specific segmentation errors.
This highlights the importance of using highquality input reconstructions and applying appropriate image quality assessment before segmentation and downstream volumetric analysis.
Automated quality control for both input images (Sanchez et al., 2024) and output segmentations will also be essential to minimise propagation of errors and uncertainty into downstream analyses.

text.text: The current framework requires reconstructed 3D T2w images with sufficient anatomical resolution and contrast and is not designed for direct segmentation of individual 2D acquisition stacks.
Application to lower-resolution clinical reconstructions will require further validation.

The parcellation protocol will be further extended to include additional structures relevant to brain development, such as the hippocampus, amygdala, midbrain, pons, nucleus accumbens, hypothalamus, choroid plexus and internal capsule, as well as finer sub-parcellation of cortical GM/WM (e.g., motor cortex).
It will also require adaptation to accommodate pathological cases with altered anatomy or the presence of additional structures (e.g., cystic lesions, tumours or haemorrhages).

Future work will also focus on improving normative modelling by incorporating Gaussian process approaches (Dimitrova et al., 2021) and subject-specific multi-factor modelling (e.g., sex, birth weight, fetal size), alongside more detailed consideration of clinical metadata in cohort selection.
text.formatted: Future work will also focus on improving normative modelling by incorporating Gaussian process approaches <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Dimitrova et al., 2021)</ref> and subject-specific multi-factor modelling (e.g., sex, birth weight, fetal size), alongside more detailed consideration of clinical metadata in cohort selection.

text.text: We will also increase the cohort of longitudinal scans across the perinatal cohort to improve our understanding of brain development.
The current results also suggest the feasibility of further extension of the subject age range to infancy and other MRI contrasts.

Finally, given the improved cortical delineation achieved by Multi-BOUNTI, extending the framework to cortical surface reconstruction and combined fetal-neonatal surface analysis represents a natural next step, building on previous work that used tissue-only BOUNTI (Uus et al., 2023) for surface extraction (Sanchez et al., 2026; Grigorescu et al., 2026).

text.text: We present Multi-BOUNTI, a unified deep learning framework for automated multi-lobe segmentation of fetal and neonatal T2w brain MRI.
The approach enables consistent parcellation across the perinatal period and provides fast, robust segmentation.

Applied to a large dHCP cohort, the pipeline enables derivation of normative volumetric growth models and supports subject-specific assessment via centiles and zscores within an automated reporting framework.
Overall, Multi-BOUNTI provides a scalable baseline solution for combined fetal and neonatal brain segmentation and volumetry, with potential for both research and clinical applications.
